conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Johnson. I’m Dr. Lee. You’re in the hospital because you were feeling very weak and lethargic, and you had an episode of vomiting. We’re trying to figure out what’s going on. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tired… sleepy. Didn’t sleep last night. Not in pain though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’re very drowsy, which we’re concerned about. We did some blood tests and found your calcium level is quite high, and your digoxin level is also elevated. These could be contributing to your confusion and fatigue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Digoxin? I take that for my heart… every other day like they said.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but in kidney disease, it can build up even with correct dosing. Your level is 2.6, which is too high. We’re going to stop it for now and talk to your cardiologist. We also found you’re very constipated, which might have caused the nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… yeah, haven’t gone in days. But I had a bowel movement after I got here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. We’ll keep an eye on that. Your calcium is 12.4, which is high. This can also make you sleepy and confused. We think it’s related to your kidney disease and possibly the vitamin D you get with dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s the plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll stop digoxin, manage your calcium with medication adjustments, and continue your regular dialysis. We’ve increased your cinacalcet dose to help with calcium. We’ll also check for other causes like infection or heart issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your CT scan shows some fluid in your lungs, likely from mild heart failure or atelectasis. No bowel obstruction, but you do have some rectal wall thickening, possibly from constipation. Your bones show changes from kidney disease—osteosclerosis and some old lesions called brown tumors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Brown tumors? Is that cancer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not cancer. In kidney disease, high calcium and PTH can cause bone changes. Your PTH is elevated but stable, so it’s likely part of your chronic condition. Hematology looked at your blood proteins and said it’s not myeloma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your digoxin level is coming down, and your mental status is a bit better. We’re still seeing some crackles in your lungs. Your oxygen is 98% on 2 liters, but we’re watching for pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been coughing. Is that pneumonia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not clearly. Your chest X-ray shows some fluid and congestion, but no focal infection yet. We’ll keep monitoring. We started benzonatate for the cough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a low-grade fever yesterday. We checked for C. diff and norovirus—both negative. Blood cultures are also negative. No sign of active infection so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a little better. Still tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your calcium is improving. We’re keeping cinacalcet at the higher dose. Your digoxin level dropped to 1.8—still coming down. We’ll repeat it soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My face cyst is draining. It hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll apply warm compresses and keep it clean. If it doesn’t improve, we may need to drain it at the bedside.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned testicular pain. We did an ultrasound. There’s a small 8mm area in your right testicle. It’s likely from old trauma, but we’ll follow up to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I sit on it sometimes in the wheelchair. Could that do it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, chronic pressure could cause that. We don’t think it’s urgent, but we’ll monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your mental status is more alert. You’re still sleepy, but you’re following conversations better. This was likely a mix of high calcium, digoxin, and poor nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I want to eat more. Can I?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re cautious. You’ve had some coughing when eating. We’ll start with softer foods and thickened liquids to reduce aspiration risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You spiked a fever two days ago and had low oxygen. Your chest X-ray showed new infiltrates on the right. We started antibiotics—vancomycin and cefepime—for possible pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt short of breath. Is it from my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but the X-ray suggests infection. Your heart function has actually improved—EF is now 55%, up from 30%. But atrial fibrillation with fast rate can still happen, especially if you desaturate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The antibiotics are finishing today. Your fever is gone, and oxygen is back to room air. But we’re still concerned about swallowing. The speech team says you aspirate thin liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but I want to eat regular food. I know the risks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We respect that. We’ll advance your diet for comfort, but we need to warn you—eating could lead to more pneumonia or heart rhythm issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I accept that. I want to live as I choose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll support your choice. We’ve updated your code status to DNR/DNI based on our discussion. Palliative care is helping with symptom control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had another fever last week. We started a new antibiotic—ceftazidime—along with vancomycin. The X-ray showed worsening right lung infiltrate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m tired of being sick. I just want to be comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re focusing on comfort now. You’re not on aggressive treatments. We’ll keep managing symptoms and infections as they come, but no ICU or intubation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest X-ray shows improvement in the right lung. We’re finishing the antibiotics. Your calcium and digoxin levels are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Any chance I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We discussed with your son. He wanted to take you in, but he can’t manage the care. So we’re looking at hospice or long-term care, but you’d prefer to eat and be comfortable here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I’ve lived my life. Just keep me out of pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You desaturated suddenly last night. The X-ray shows worsening right pneumonia. We’re restarting vancomycin and cefepime for HCAP coverage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was eating… I know it’s risky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and each time you aspirate, it can trigger a rhythm problem or infection. But you understand and accept that. We’ll continue supporting your choice.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The infection is responding. Your oxygen is better. The X-ray shows less consolidation. We’re almost done with antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had a few more episodes of low oxygen after eating. Each time, your heart goes into afib with fast rate. It’s dangerous, but you’re choosing to continue eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. But food is one of the few things I enjoy now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep your symptoms managed. Palliative is helping with comfort meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been stable for a while. Your labs are better. Calcium is down, digoxin is 1.5—safe now. But your overall condition is fragile.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready for this to be over. I don’t want more tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We won’t do more tests. We’ll keep you comfortable. If you get worse, we’ll use medications to ease breathing and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve developed abdominal pain and vomiting. The X-ray shows possible small bowel obstruction. We could place a tube or consider surgery, but that’s not what you want.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No tubes, no surgery. Just keep me comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make you NPO and start a Dilaudid drip for comfort. This is now comfort-focused care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very weak today. Your blood pressure is low, and you’re not eating. We’re continuing comfort care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you… for listening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The X-ray confirms small bowel obstruction. But we’re not intervening. We’re focused on keeping you pain-free.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very quiet today. We’re here with you. Your breathing is slow, but you’re not in distress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your family is here. We’re all supporting you through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re peaceful. We’re not doing anything to prolong this. You’re not suffering.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson passed away peacefully overnight with family present. He was comfortable until the end.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll notify the family and begin discharge procedures for hospice care.
